newsitem.title: SPAIN: Latam growth could jump with in-depth reforms.
newsitem.headline: Latam growth could jump with in-depth reforms.

text.p: Latin American economic growth rates could jump to levels similar to the fast-growing Southeastern Asian "tigers" if nations undertake in-depth reform and boost education spending.

The regional growth rate could climb to eight percent in a decade with tax and labour reform, privatisations and better education, according to a study published on Sunday by the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB).

The study, presented by chief IADB economist Ricardo Hausmann before the opening of the IADB's annual board of governors meeting on Monday, evaluates the effects of economic reforms initiated over the past 10 years.
According to the study, those countries that moved most rapidly to free-market measures on commercial and financial reform had advanced most rapidly economically.
The reforms also reduced exchange-rate volatility, but did not manage to stabilise regional growth which continued to suffer ups and downs.
"The reforms have helped, but more needs to be done to ensure the macroeconomic stability required for acclerated and more equitable long-run growth in the region," the study said.
The distribution of income in Latin America remained the most unequal in the world, although the concentration of wealth has not increased over this period, the study showed.
Poverty in the region stabilised during the decade at about 150 million people, reaching one in every three inhabitant.
Without the reforms unndertaken in most countries of Latin American, per capita income would now be 20 percent lower at $2,400 a year instead of the current $3,000, the report added.
Despite statistical evidence of improvement, the IADB found broad-based pessimism among citizens.
In an opinion poll, seventy-five percent of those surveyed said they believed poverty had risen during the last 10 years, while 61 percent saw no improvement.

And Latin Americans were divided in their perception of the proper economic model to follow - with about the same number backing a system of private enterprise as those who supported a mixed state or a worker co-management model.
Not all governments had adopted reforms recommended by the IADB and in some case they had hardly been put into practice.
While almost all had opted to liberalise finanical and commercial markets, a smaller number had made progress on tax reform and privatisations and only a very few had addressed labour reform.

Education progressed more slowly in Latin American than in the rest of the world. According to the IADB, although they began at the same level two decades ago, the Asian labour force now has an average of nine years of education while Latin America has just five years.

If these objectives are completed, countries like Ecuador, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Colombia, the Dominican Republic and Paraguay could have annual growth rates of between six and eight percent of gross domestic product.
